Or, if you know much about the background of this case, you could also call him Ignored Witness. Because that nickname could apply to many witnesses in this case, we will stick with “Alpena Witness.” The audio files of an interview of Alpena Witness tell the story better than I ever could. They first four segments of eight are posted below. This interview is timely at this stage, given recent posts.
After the revelations about Bloomfield Township/Village Officer Richard McNamee, convicted pedophile, we are once again focused on the one square mile enclave of Bloomfield Village where Chris Busch lived with his parents and John Hastings lived a stone’s throw away in a home owned by his parents. McNamee lived a three-minute car ride away at 423 S. Cranbrook Cross, Bloomfield Hills. To my knowledge, no one in law enforcement has acted on this recent lead about McNamee or contacted the victim who came forward.
We also visited the conclusions concerning the 2009 polygraph of Chris Busch’s neighbor, John Hastings, in a recent post. https://catherinebroad.blog/.../does-this-sound-like.../ We know it was Hastings because, although his name was mostly redacted from the MSP documents, they followed a handwritten title page entitled John Hastings Investigation. No, I am not kidding.
We’ve compared photos to the composite drawing from 1977 that was withheld from the public. https://catherinebroad.blog/.../the.../comment-page-1/
I think you will find it very helpful at this point to consider the following interview of “Alpena Witness,” who overheard John Hastings speaking to Helen Dagner on December 26, 1991, about the OCCK crimes. Just listen carefully and it will all make sense. My gratitude to Andy Berthiaume who has been working on a podcast series about these crimes for the past few years for sharing the interview. Andy hopes to have the series completed in the next few months. And my thanks to Alpena Witness as well, for revisiting the nightmare he got swept into in his lengthy interview with Andy. I believe the interview took place in early November 2018.

Original comment not found in the scraped archive.
My LH CSI assessment—
At the time of the attack, Faraday and Jensen are parked at the turnout when the perpetrator pulls in, positioning his vehicle just to the right of the passenger-side door. He opens his door and immediately fires a single round into the air to frighten the victims and gain control—ejecting a casing which bounces off the roof of his car and lands on the opposite side of his vehicle approximately 20 feet away from the primary cluster of casings. This likely accounts for the missing slug noted at the scene.
The perpetrator then orders both victims to exit their vehicle through the passenger side—Betty Lou emerging first, followed closely by David. Upon exiting, David immediately attempts to disarm the gunman, pushing the weapon upward and to his right. During the struggle, the firearm discharges into the sheet metal above the rear passenger window at close range. This casing ejects to the right of the firearm at a downward angle, bouncing off the open passenger door and into the passenger front floorboard.
The physical confrontation continues along the side of David’s Rambler, where a second round is fired through the rear window at an estimated 43-degree angle, striking the interior of the opposite wheel well. The perpetrator quickly regains control, subduing David near the rear passenger-side tire. In a manner consistent with the behavior later reported at Lake Berryessa, the assailant falsely reassures the victims, stating that he only intends to rob them and that no one will be harmed. This brief pause disrupts David’s fight-or-flight response.
Seizing the opportunity, the perpetrator then fires a round from David’s left side, striking him behind the left ear. David immediately collapses face-up. At this point, Betty Lou, realizing David has been shot, attempts to flee toward the road in the direction of Vallejo, passing the perpetrator to his right and at close range. He immediately fires a round at her back at close proximity—accounting for the single grain of embedded gunpowder in the back of her dress—before discharging additional rounds into the upper-right quadrant of her back as she staggers forward. Betty Lou collapses approximately 28 feet from the rear bumper of the vehicle and succumbs to her injuries shortly thereafter.
This again is my personal assessment based on what I see .

Alex Baber
Sunday, June 8, 2025 at 3:14 PM · Zodiac Killer Suspects
View comment ↗ View post ↗
From a practical standpoint, it is my opinion that the perpetrator likely had minimal blood exposure under the established circumstances. The firearm appears to have been placed nearly flush against the right temple of the victim, and the factory-installed full front seat of the Mercury Galaxie would have served as a partial barrier. Notably, the seat itself exhibits limited blood staining compared to the more substantial pooling observed on the floorboard and adjacent dashboard area, as seen in the crime scene photographs.
The perpetrator left behind gloves, suggesting he may have had no concern regarding latent prints—likely due to the use of airplane cement applied to his fingertips, as implied in his 10/13 letter and by the visible bloody prints lacking clear cores. Any blood spatter on outer clothing, such as the sleeves, could have been easily concealed by a windbreaker, which aligns with witness descriptions and may have been donned after the act of shooting.
Regarding footwear, blood on the soles would only be expected if the perpetrator had stepped in the pool of blood outside the passenger door role had it drip down onto the top of when accessing the passenger side door—an unlikely scenario given the victim’s position upon being discovered. Stine was found face down on the passenger-side floorboard, with his lower body still partially draped over the bench seat toward the driver’s side, suggesting he collapsed immediately upon being shot, obviously. It appears the Zodiac then pulled Stine fully into the passenger footwell area, as indicated by the upward displacement of the victim’s shirt, which would have allowed access to cut the swath from the back of the garment.
Later, Officer Armand Pelissetti repositioned Stine onto his back on the passenger seat for examination of life. Based on the positioning of the body and the absence of significant blood transfer patterns on the surrounding surfaces, it is reasonable to conclude that the Zodiac had minimal direct blood exposure. This would account for Fouke not identifying any visually whether he stopped him or not—which I believe he did based on some specifics Donald previewed in his “scratch” nearly A MONTH after the incident coupled with Zodiac’s follow up letter calling him out on such.

This assessment is further supported by the suspect’s use of language, such as referring to his victims as “boy” and “girl,” which reflects generational speech patterns more commonly associated with an older individual. His overall linguistic profile similarly suggests a man of more advanced age as well.
It is likely Zodiac committed his first murder in his early twenties, the level of tactical awareness he demonstrated—both in planning and execution—suggests a degree of training and discipline consistent with prior military experience. In my assessment, it is likely he was a World War II veteran and familiar with death, given the methods employed and the behavioral indicators observed throughout the case.

It’s time to address the elephant in the room: in my personal view, criminal profiling often resembles a carnival sideshow—like the performer who guesses your age or weight. While it may appear insightful on the surface, profiling is primarily an attempt to predict definitive traits based on “behavioral evidence,” making it both counterintuitive and inherently speculative as serial killers often use different means. At times, it borders on the silly—have you ever read Douglas’ Unabomber profile?
Yes, modus operandi (MO) can occasionally be useful, and behavioral “signatures” may offer intriguing leads during an investigation—on occasion. However, despite its glorification in popular media, including shows like Mindhunter, the actual accuracy of criminal profiling remains historically low, with successful predictions occurring in fewer than 25% of cases.
Although some serial offenders may draw influence—directly or indirectly—from prior offenders, no two are ever truly alike. Each exhibits a distinct set of motivations, compulsions, and unique kill patterns, underscoring the limitations of relying too heavily on profiling as an investigative tool.

i think he did obviously have a territory he did his canonical kills in but I wouldn’t jump the conclusion he was a permanent resident at that time. The weekends and holidays timing could be contained by someone who took a lot of vacations and weekends in that area but didn’t necessarily live there all the time. It would be a clever move to use an area which you know well like a ‘home from home’ to kill in but don’t actually permanently live in 90% of the year. Just by your permanent address being a few hours away you could drastically reduce the chances of being recognised compared to killing on your own doorstep. Steve Watkins Anything is possible—hopefully we know one day for sure.
Arthur Leigh Allen presents as a compelling suspect at first glance, largely due to the sustained public narrative fueled by Don Chaney’s fabricated lies because Allen touched his daughter and reinforced by the 1986 Zodiac book by Robert Gray-Smith. However, upon closer examination, Allen fails to meet critical thresholds. He is the only known suspect to have been definitively ruled out by three of the five primary forensic categories—two of them on multiple occasions.
While elements like the Zodiac watch story and the so-called death letter confession make for dramatic television, the latter did not occur as commonly described in the public domain. In truth, Allen was unable to write with his left hand, a core characteristic attributed to the Zodiac. He was not stopped with a knife on the day of the Lake Berryessa attack; and according to multiple independent sources, the weapon used in that murder was not a conventional knife, but rather a bayonet or similar instrument.
Additionally, contrary to the widely circulated claim, Allen did not call in sick the day after Cheri Jo Bates’ 1966 murder—he called off work the day after that. While Allen was undeniably a disturbed individual with a history of child molestation, the available evidence does not substantiate his involvement in the Zodiac crimes.

What is justice?
Stephen Thornthwaite Excellent question, Stephen—Justice is a concept that often evades a single, universal definition. For many, it holds a deeply personal meaning—shaped by individual values, experiences, and perceptions of right and wrong. It is frequently mistaken for retribution or vengeance, though the two are not synonymous. Some may see justice as a moral obligation to restore balance or uphold fairness, while others interpret it through the lens of honor, righteousness, or societal order. In some narratives, justice may even be served by an anti-hero—someone who operates outside conventional norms but seeks to correct a perceived wrong nonetheless. Ultimately, it can be many things to many people based on their beliefs and/or position even.

What does the evidence show?
Sloane Golden Unfortunately, the cited source is inaccurate. The first officially recognized victim, Edward Smith, was shot with a .22 LR round, believed to have been fired from a semiautomatic pistol. Two additional victims were stabbed, while the cause of death for several others could not be determined due to advanced decomposition and the loss of body parts, likely from scavenger activity.
The evidence used to convict Wayne Williams would not meet the threshold of admissibility in a courtroom today. This includes the so-called “tri-fiber” evidence, which was both circumstantial and would be considered inconclusive. Furthermore, the use of dog hairs allegedly matching those found at the crime scene is highly questionable, especially given that the canine unit used to locate the body was of the same species—creating a clear risk of contamination.
Recent DNA testing, which progressed approximately halfway through the evidence, failed to connect Wayne Williams to any of the victims. In fact, several samples revealed the presence of unidentified Caucasian DNA. I can attest to this personally, as I was directly involved in the case review. Investigative practices from the early 1980s were rudimentary by today’s forensic standards.

Patricia Bennet I’m limited in what I can share at this time. However, I can confirm that an incident from the 1970s involving the suspect and his stepchild resurfaced after key connections were made within the family. At that point, a descendant realized they had, for decades, unknowingly been in possession of physical evidence related to the case—this ties directly into the earlier mention regarding other potent sources of DNA outside of envelopes—particularly victims.
We immediately documented and photographed the materials before transferring them to California law enforcement, who are now leading the investigation. At this stage, both my team and some active jurisdictions involved in California have a strong sense of who the Zodiac was. We’re now following the appropriate procedures required for verification before public disclosure.
Some individuals here were remarkably close in their assessments—others, not even in the ballpark. My recent trip to California was part of this process, during which I met with the proper representatives of LE with liaisons as part of the ongoing coordination.
The cases that are connected to him are LH, BR, LB, Presidio, and Oceanside—
Bates is a possible outlier that is being looked at closer based on the new findings—
Lass, Dominguez, & Edward’s are currently excluded—
There are two additional homicides that can be connected, from the suspect himself, discovered within his belongings.
I can assure the reader that this new evidence is neither coincidental nor speculative. It is not built on vague interpretations—such as a scar imagined in a composite sketch—or on hundreds of unrelated spent shell casings. It does not stem from false accusations made by disgruntled acquaintances, glorified tales of a bloody knife found in a car when the actual weapon was a bayonet, or sensationalized stories involving school skipping murder sprees with children present.
This suspect’s story doesn’t rely on fiction. It’s grounded in obsession and an insatiable need for control. Ultimately, it is the “why” that is most disturbing in my opinion. I look forward to the close of this horrific story.

Fouke and Zelms did not document the encounter in their original report—likely for obvious reasons. However, according to Investigator Harvey Hines’ detailed report (see Page 31), Inspector Dave Toschi interviewed both officers and later confirmed the incident to Hines. Given that Hines’ report states “according to Toschi” directly, and was reviewed by LE officials across multiple jurisdictions—none of whom refuted the account or challenged the report that Fouke and Zelms had spoken with the suspect—I have no reason to doubt the credibility of Toschi’s statement as documented during Hines interaction with him.
And for the record, this account was documented by Inspector David Toschi; however, that information is not accessible to the general public. This includes authors, producers, reporters, family members, victim advocates, podcasters, armchair sleuths, and so-called “Zodiologists”—or whatever term they prefer. And frankly, it shouldn’t be. In my review, I’ve witnessed the facts in this case repeatedly distorted or manipulated once released publicly—so I’m in full agreement with SFPD.

Alex Baber there was no real evidence. That case would have gone nowhere and it would have put the family through hell. The fact that it was presented was BS. It doesn’t take much at all to get an indictment.
Patrick Apoian There was both physical and circumstantial evidence involved here, Pat—the ransom letter; the indentation on the writing pad for which it was composed; the note’s discarded draft in the kitchen can naming both parents rather than only John; the double over knot passed off as a garrote though it had no means of slippage; the broken paintbrush discovered in Patsy’s pale; her blanket and Barbie pajamas; the conflicting accounts between first responder French’s initial witness statements and their accounts provided later; the endless contradictions within the various depositions, ￼and the inconsistency between John’s claim to have read a bedtime story to JonBenét and Burke and then the assertion that she arrived home asleep from the Fleet residence and was carried directly to bed. The pineapple and milk documented on the dining room table then discovered in her intestinal tract though both parents claim she wasn’t awake to consume it nor how it even got there replying only “we don’t know?”
Perhaps this case required a far more rigorous and unyielding pursuit of the truth or “hell,” particularly given that the life of a six-year-old child was taken.
And Alex Hunter’s out & out lying about the grand jury’s decision is both disgraceful and shameful.
